subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = 2S, then prove that cos(S−A) + cos(S−B) + cos(S−C) + cos S = 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2).

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.108 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 170. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's own inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: classed LAQ on its length and shape — a transformation identity on a triangle, the exact shape of Unit 6's own LAQ chapter. The bank prints no mark cut, so this classification is OURS. Printed appearances: TS 18. FOUR terms, so they pair off — and the pairing is chosen so that the shared letter cancels. Pair the first two together and the last two together. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular split for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Simplify the second pair.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Pair the four terms
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks. Bracket the first two and the last two, then apply cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C+D)/2) cos((C−D)/2) to each.
steps.memory_tip: FOUR terms: bracket the first two and the last two, then apply the cosine sum formula to each.

recall.must_convey: That the four terms are paired as (first two) and (last two), and cos C + cos D is applied to each.
accept: pair the first two and the last two then apply the cos plus cos formula to each pair
bracket them two by two and use the sum to product formula
apply the formula twice, once to each pair

pair the four terms and convert each

steps.why: Pairing the first with the third instead would leave A and C mixed, and neither half would simplify. The pairing is chosen for what cancels.
common_mistakes: Pairing the first with the last.
Applying the formula to three terms at once.

steps.label: Simplify the first pair
steps.margin_note: Two marks. From A + B + C = 2S, 2S − A − B = C, so the first cosine is cos(C/2). The other is cos((B−A)/2), which equals cos((A−B)/2).
steps.memory_tip: 2S − A − B = C, so the first cosine is cos(C/2). And cos(−θ) = cos θ.
lines: A + B + C = 2S ⇒ 2S − A − B = C

recall.must_convey: That 2S − A − B = C makes the first cosine cos(C/2), and cos((B−A)/2) = cos((A−B)/2).
accept: two S minus A minus B is C so the first cosine is cos C by two, and the sign inside the other cosine does not matter
the condition turns the messy angle into C by two

two S minus A minus B ante C, cos C by two
simplify the first pair using the condition
heard_as: two S minus A minus B

steps.why: Rearranging the given condition is what makes the substitution possible — 2S − A − B is not obviously C until the condition is written the other way round.
common_mistakes: Writing 2S − A − B as C/2 directly.
Keeping the minus inside the second cosine as if it mattered.

steps.label: Simplify the second pair
steps.margin_note: Two marks (fifth and sixth). (2S − C)/2 = (A + B)/2, and cos(−C/2) = cos(C/2). Both pairs now carry cos(C/2).
steps.memory_tip: (2S − C)/2 = (A + B)/2, and cos(−C/2) = cos(C/2). Both pairs now carry cos(C/2).
lines: 2S − C = A + B ⇒ cos((2S − C)/2) = cos((A+B)/2)

recall.must_convey: That (2S − C)/2 = (A+B)/2 and cos(−C/2) = cos(C/2), so the second pair is 2 cos((A+B)/2) cos(C/2).
accept: two S minus C is A plus B so that cosine is cos of A plus B by two, and the minus inside the other drops
the second pair also carries cos C by two
both pairs now share cos C by two
two S minus C ante A plus B, so cos A plus B by two
simplify the second pair

steps.why: Both pairs ending with cos(C/2) is not luck — it is why this pairing was chosen, and it is what allows the next factoring.
common_mistakes: Writing 2S − C as A + B + C.

steps.label: Take 2 cos(C/2) common
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Both pairs have 2 cos(C/2), so pull it out — leaving a sum of two cosines inside.
steps.memory_tip: Both pairs share 2 cos(C/2) — pull it out, leaving a SUM of two cosines inside.

recall.must_convey: That 2 cos(C/2) is factored out, leaving cos((A−B)/2) + cos((A+B)/2) inside.
accept: both pairs have two cos C by two so take it out leaving a sum of two cosines
factor out two cos C by two
the bracket is cos of A minus B by two plus cos of A plus B by two

take the common factor out

steps.why: The right-hand side has cos(C/2) as one of its three factors — pulling it out now means the bracket only has to produce the other two.
common_mistakes: Factoring only cos(C/2) and losing the 2.

steps.label: Apply the formula again
steps.margin_note: Last mark. cos X + cos Y with X = (A−B)/2, Y = (A+B)/2 gives 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) — the same formula used in step 1.
steps.memory_tip: The same formula as step 1, now with X = (A−B)/2 and Y = (A+B)/2.

lines.text: ∴ The sum equals 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2)

recall.must_convey: That the bracket is 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2), giving 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2).
accept: the bracket becomes two cos A by two into cos B by two so the total is four cos A by two cos B by two cos C by two

steps.why: The half-angles come out because the formula halves the sum and difference of two angles that were already halves. Three uses of one formula finish the whole proof.
